text: DROP TABLE is one of the most permanent operations in all of T-SQL. It removes a table's structure — its columns, its constraints, its indexes — and every row of data stored in it, all at once. There's no undo short of restoring a backup.

Drop table dbo dot LessonDemo. Gone — structure and data, together. Running this against a table that doesn't exist raises an error and stops your script, which is exactly the problem the next form solves.

Drop table if exists dbo dot LessonDemo. This quietly does nothing if the table was never there, and drops it if it was. That makes it the safe choice at the top of setup scripts, where you often want a guaranteed clean slate before creating a table fresh.

This fails, because LessonChild's foreign key still references LessonParent. A table can't be dropped while something else still depends on it — a foreign key from another table, or a view built on top of it. SQL Server refuses the drop rather than silently leaving another object broken.

You've already seen TRUNCATE TABLE earlier in this course. Truncate table empties a table but leaves it standing, ready for new rows. Drop table removes the table itself — there's nothing left to insert into until you create it again.
Next lesson: IDENTITY columns and SCOPE_IDENTITY — auto-incrementing keys, and the one safe way to read the value you just inserted back.
